build_target.title: What Does "Building" Mean?
build_target.html:
When you write code, you write instructions for a computer. But computers don't understand English or code directly — they understand machine code: binary instructions specific to their CPU.

Building (or compiling) is the process of translating your source code into something the computer can actually execute. The output might be a standalone binary (.exe on Windows, no extension on Linux/macOS), or source code in another language.

Different languages build differently — some produce binaries ahead of time, some translate code on the fly, and some run through an interpreter.

build_target.title: AOT Compilation — Ahead of Time
build_target.html:
AOT (Ahead-of-Time) compilation means your code is fully translated to machine code before it runs. The result is a standalone binary — a file you can double-click and it just runs, with no other software needed.

Languages that use AOT: C, C++, Rust, and UniLogic when targeting native platforms.

Advantages: Fast execution — the CPU runs instructions directly. No startup overhead.

Disadvantage: The binary is tied to a specific platform (you can't take a Windows binary and run it on macOS).

build_target.title: JIT Compilation — Just in Time
build_target.html:
JIT (Just-in-Time) compilation means the code is compiled while it runs. The runtime starts interpreting or compiling code on the fly as each function is called.

Languages that use JIT: Java (JVM), JavaScript (V8 engine), C# (.NET CLR).

Advantages: Can optimise based on actual runtime behaviour. Code is more portable — the same bytecode runs anywhere a JIT runtime is installed.

Disadvantages: Slower startup (the JIT needs to warm up). Peak performance is usually lower than AOT-compiled code.

build_target.title: OS and ISA — Why Downloads Ask What System You Have
build_target.html:
There are two key dimensions to a platform:

OS (Operating System) — Windows, macOS, Linux. Each has its own system calls (ways to ask the OS to open files, create windows, connect to the network). A Windows binary calls Windows APIs. A Linux binary calls Linux APIs. They are not interchangeable.

ISA (Instruction Set Architecture) — the CPU's language. x64 (also called x86-64 or AMD64) is used by most Intel and AMD desktop CPUs. ARM64 (also called AArch64) is used by Apple Silicon Macs, most phones, and newer Windows laptops. A binary compiled for x64 will not run on ARM64.

Platform = OS + ISA. "Windows x64" is one platform. "macOS ARM64" is a different platform. This is why download pages ask which OS you have, and offer "x64" or "ARM" variants.

build_target.title: ABI — The Contract Between Program and OS
build_target.html:
ABI (Application Binary Interface) is the low-level contract that defines how a program talks to the operating system and to other libraries at the binary level.

It specifies things like: how function arguments are passed (in registers? on the stack?), how data structures are laid out in memory, how system calls are made, and how the stack is managed.

This is why you can't copy a Windows .exe to Linux and run it — even if both machines use x64 CPUs, the ABI is completely different. The system calls, the calling conventions, the runtime libraries — all different.

ABI compatibility is also why library updates sometimes require recompiling your program: if a library changes its ABI (how it exports functions), old compiled code breaks.

build_target.title: Python — Write Once, Run Anywhere (With Python Installed)
build_target.html:
Python is an interpreted language. When you run a .py file, the Python interpreter reads your code and executes it directly.

Because the interpreter handles all platform differences, your .py file runs on Windows, macOS, or Linux without any changes — as long as Python is installed.

Tradeoff: Interpreted code is slower than native binaries. Every time you run the script, the interpreter re-reads and re-executes it (though Python does cache .pyc bytecode files to skip re-parsing).

This portability is why Python is so popular for scripting and data science — you share a .py file and it just works on any machine.

build_target.title: Java's JVM — Write Once, Run Anywhere
build_target.html:
Java introduced the motto "write once, run anywhere." Java source code is compiled to bytecode (a platform-neutral intermediate format), which runs on the JVM (Java Virtual Machine).

The JVM is available on every major OS. The same .jar file runs on Windows, macOS, and Linux without modification — the JVM handles platform differences.

Several other languages also compile to JVM bytecode: Kotlin (Android's main language), Scala, Groovy, Clojure.

The JVM uses JIT compilation — bytecode is compiled to native machine code at runtime for fast execution.

build_target.title: WASM — WebAssembly
build_target.html:
WebAssembly (WASM) is a binary instruction format that runs in any modern web browser. You compile your code to WASM, host it on a web server, and users open your app in a browser — no install required.

WASM runs at near-native speed and is supported by Chrome, Firefox, Safari, and Edge. Languages that can compile to WASM include C, C++, Rust, and UniLogic.

Why it matters: Traditionally, complex apps (games, video editors, CAD tools) required a native install. WASM lets them run in a browser tab. Figma, Google Earth, and AutoCAD web all use WASM.

WASM is sandboxed — it can't access the filesystem or OS directly without explicit browser APIs. This makes it very secure.

build_target.title: UniLogic VM Target — Bytecode
build_target.html:
UniLogic can compile your code to UL bytecode — an intermediate format that runs on the UniLogic VM, similar to Python bytecode on CPython or Java bytecode on the JVM.

The UL VM is lightweight and portable. Anywhere the VM is installed, your bytecode runs — across Windows, macOS, and Linux without recompiling.

This is the "distribution without commit to a single platform" option: ship one bytecode file and let users run it on their VM.

build_target.title: How Code Clarity Builds
build_target.html:
OS only → produces an installer that includes both x64 and ARM64 variants. The installer detects the user's ISA at install time and installs the right binary. Use this for broad distribution.

OS + ISA → produces a single native binary for exactly that platform. No installer — just the binary. Use this when you know your target exactly.

Cannot choose ISA alone — ISA is meaningless without an OS. You must choose an OS first.

Bundling runtimes: Code Clarity can bundle C, Python, or Rust runtimes into the output so users don't need to install them. Set runtime paths in File > Settings.

memory.title: RAM vs Disk
memory.html:
Your computer has two main kinds of storage:

RAM (Random Access Memory) — fast, temporary. Data in RAM is lost when power is cut. RAM is where your programs and data live while they run. Modern computers have 8–64 GB of RAM.

Disk (SSD or HDD) — slow, permanent. Files stay on disk when you power off. Disk is where programs are installed and where your files live permanently. Modern computers have 256 GB to several TB of disk.

The key difference: RAM is 10–100x faster than disk for sequential reads, and millions of times faster for random access. Everything that needs to happen quickly must be in RAM.

memory.title: What "Memory" Means in Programming
memory.html:
When programmers say "memory", they almost always mean RAM, not disk space. "Memory leak" means RAM that was allocated but never freed. "Out of memory" means the program ran out of RAM.

Disk space is called "disk", "storage", or "filesystem" — never just "memory".

This matters because the constraints are very different: you might have 16 GB of RAM but 1 TB of disk. Filling disk is easy to notice (downloads fail); filling RAM causes the system to slow to a crawl.

memory.title: Binary Size on Disk
memory.html:
When your program is compiled, it produces a binary file (or script) stored on disk. This is the binary size — how much space the program takes up as a file.

A larger binary takes longer to download, longer to copy, and longer to initially load. For desktop apps this rarely matters. For mobile apps, web apps, or embedded systems, it matters a lot — users abandon downloads that take too long.

Binary size is influenced by: how much code you have, whether debug symbols are included, which libraries are statically linked in, and whether the binary is stripped (debug info removed for release builds).

Code Clarity shows you the binary size before you run the program, so you can spot unexpectedly large outputs early.

memory.title: RAM at Runtime
memory.html:
When your program runs, the OS loads it into RAM and starts executing. Variables, objects, arrays, strings — everything your program creates at runtime lives in RAM.

RAM usage grows as your program creates more data and shrinks as it frees data. How it grows and shrinks depends on the language:

- C / C++: Manual control. You call malloc() to allocate and free() to release. Forget to free = memory leak.

- Python / Java / Go: Garbage collected. The runtime automatically finds and frees data that's no longer reachable.

- Rust: Ownership model. The compiler tracks lifetimes and inserts free calls automatically — no GC, no leaks.

memory.title: Demand Paging — Your Program Is NOT Fully in RAM
memory.html:
Here is something that surprises many developers: your entire program is not loaded into RAM at once.

The OS uses a technique called demand paging (also called virtual memory). RAM is divided into 4 KB chunks called pages. The OS only loads a page into RAM when your program actually tries to access it. Everything else stays on disk.

If you have a 100 MB program but your current execution path only touches 2 MB of code and data, only those pages are in RAM. The rest are on disk, waiting to be loaded if ever needed.

This is why programs can run even if they're larger than available RAM — the OS swaps pages in and out as needed. But if too many pages are needed at once, the OS frantically swaps pages between RAM and disk. This is called thrashing and it makes everything slow.

memory.title: Why Memory Efficiency Matters
memory.html:
If your program uses more RAM than the system has available, the OS starts swapping — moving pages from RAM to disk to make room. Disk access is millions of times slower than RAM, so performance collapses.

On mobile and embedded systems, there's often no swap at all. If you exceed available RAM, the OS kills your process outright (OOM killer).

Memory efficiency also matters for server software: if each user session uses 50 MB of RAM, a 16 GB server handles only ~320 concurrent users. Cut it to 5 MB and you serve 3,200 users on the same hardware.

Code Clarity tracks your program's RAM usage over time so you can catch leaks, unexpected spikes, and runaway growth before they hit production.

memory.title: Stack vs Heap
memory.html:
When your program runs, RAM is divided into regions. The two most important are:

Stack — fast, automatic. Local variables in a function live on the stack. When a function returns, its stack frame is popped and that memory is instantly reclaimed. No bookkeeping needed. The stack is small (typically 1–8 MB per thread).

Heap — flexible, manual (or GC'd). Objects you create dynamically (new in C++/Java, malloc in C, all Python objects) live on the heap. The heap can grow to fill available RAM, but allocation is slower than the stack and the memory must be explicitly freed (or garbage collected).

Python: almost everything goes on the heap — even small integers. This is convenient but costs RAM. C: local variables go on the stack, heap only when you call malloc(). This is efficient but requires discipline.

security.title: What Is a Vulnerability?
security.html:
A vulnerability is a weakness in code that an attacker can exploit. It might be a bug, a missing check, an unsafe assumption, or a dangerous pattern.

Vulnerabilities are the standard term in the security industry. When you hear about a CVE (Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures number), it's a publicly disclosed vulnerability in a piece of software.

Most vulnerabilities don't come from malicious developers — they come from honest mistakes: forgetting to check the length of input, trusting data from the network, or using an unsafe function that's been known to be dangerous for decades.

The goal of security testing is to find these weaknesses before attackers do.

security.title: How Attackers Exploit Applications
security.html:
A typical attack follows this pattern:

1. Find a vulnerability — automated scanners, manual code review, or checking known CVE databases for the libraries you use.

2. Craft a malicious input — a specially constructed string, file, or network packet designed to trigger the weakness.

3. Achieve the goal:

- Read data — steal passwords, API keys, user data

- Modify data — change records, corrupt files

- Execute code — run arbitrary commands on the server

- Crash the system — denial of service

Good security testing simulates steps 1 and 2 in a controlled way so you can fix weaknesses before real attackers find them.

security.title: Buffer Overflows
security.html:
A buffer overflow occurs when code writes more data into a fixed-size buffer than the buffer can hold, overwriting adjacent memory.

In C and C++, buffers are just contiguous memory regions. If you have a 64-byte array and write 128 bytes into it, the extra 64 bytes overwrite whatever is next in memory — which might be another variable, a saved register, or the return address on the stack.

An attacker can craft input that overwrites the return address with the address of attacker-controlled code. When the function returns, execution jumps to the attacker's code. This is called a stack smashing attack and is the classic buffer overflow exploit.

Buffer overflows are the #1 source of security vulnerabilities in C/C++ code. Modern mitigations (stack canaries, ASLR, NX bits) make exploitation harder but not impossible.

Rust's ownership model and bounds checking prevent buffer overflows entirely at compile time.

security.title: SQL Injection
security.html:
SQL injection is one of the most common and dangerous web vulnerabilities. It occurs when user-supplied input is inserted directly into a database query without being sanitised.

Example — a login query built by string concatenation:

SELECT * FROM users WHERE name='" + username + "'

If the user types ' OR '1'='1 as their username, the query becomes:

SELECT * FROM users WHERE name='' OR '1'='1'

This returns all users — the attacker is now logged in as the first user in the database, typically an admin.

Fix: Always use parameterised queries (prepared statements). Never build SQL by concatenating strings with user input.

security.title: Code Injection
security.html:
Code injection happens when user input is executed as code. The classic examples are functions like eval(), exec(), and os.system() in Python, or eval() in JavaScript.

If your program does:

os.system("ping " + user_input)

An attacker enters google.com; rm -rf / and your server deletes itself.

The same applies to shell commands built from user input, template engines that execute code, and any deserialization of untrusted data.

Fix: Never pass user input to functions that execute code or shell commands. Use library functions with argument arrays instead of shell strings (subprocess.run(["ping", user_input]) is safe; os.system("ping " + user_input) is not).

security.title: SAST — Static Application Security Testing
security.html:
SAST analyzes your source code without running it. It reads your code line by line, looking for known dangerous patterns, missing checks, and calls to unsafe functions.

Think of it as a security expert reviewing your code. It can find buffer overflows, SQL injection, code injection, hardcoded secrets, missing input validation, and more — all without needing to run the program.

Advantages: Runs fast, works on incomplete code, catches issues early in development.

Limitations: Can produce false positives (flagging safe code as dangerous) and can miss runtime-only issues (bugs that only appear with specific inputs).

In Code Clarity, SAST runs on the Static Analysis tab.

security.title: DAST — Dynamic Application Security Testing
security.html:
DAST runs your compiled program and sends it malicious inputs to see what breaks. Think of it as a controlled hacking attempt — your own program being attacked in a safe environment.

DAST sends attack inputs like buffer-overflow strings, SQL injection payloads, extremely large inputs, and malformed data. It watches for crashes, unexpected output, memory errors, and information leaks.

Advantages: Finds real vulnerabilities that only appear at runtime. No false positives — if the program crashes on a specific input, that's a real bug.

Limitations: Requires a compiled executable. Can't find issues in code paths not exercised by the test inputs. Slower than SAST.

In Code Clarity, DAST runs on the Dynamic Testing tab. Build your program first, then run DAST.

security.title: SAST and DAST Together
security.html:
SAST and DAST are complementary — neither is sufficient alone.

SAST catches issues early, works without running the program, and scans 100% of code paths. Use it continuously during development.

DAST confirms real exploitability and finds runtime-only issues that static analysis misses. Use it before releases and on CI/CD pipelines.

Professional security teams use both, plus manual code review and penetration testing. For most projects, SAST + DAST catches the majority of common vulnerabilities.

The security testing tools in this window implement both: the Static Analysis tab on the left runs SAST, the Dynamic Testing tab on the right runs DAST.

code_health.title: What Is Code Health?
code_health.html:
Code health describes how easy your code is to understand, change, and test. Healthy code has low complexity, clear names, no repeated blocks, and no unused code. Unhealthy code grows slowly harder to work with — every change risks breaking something because the code is tangled, repeated, or opaque.

Code health doesn't mean the code is wrong — it can produce correct results and still be difficult to maintain. The problems show up when you try to add a feature, fix a bug, or onboard someone new.

The five metrics in Code Clarity's health check — Complexity, Readability, Duplication, Dead Code, and Naming — cover the main dimensions of code quality recognised by the industry.

code_health.title: Cyclomatic Complexity
code_health.html:
Cyclomatic complexity measures how many independent execution paths run through a function. It was defined by Thomas McCabe in 1976 and remains the standard metric today.

Every time your code branches — if, else if, for, while, case, &&, ||, catch — the count goes up by 1. Start at 1 and add 1 per decision point. That's the cyclomatic complexity.

Score 1–9: simple, easy to test. Each path through the function can be covered with a handful of tests.

Score 10–15: moderately complex. Testing becomes effort-intensive. Consider splitting the function.

Score >15: high complexity. The function is almost certainly doing too much. Refactor into smaller functions with single responsibilities.

High complexity is the single strongest predictor of defect density in code.

code_health.title: Readability — Length and Nesting
code_health.html:
Function length is the simplest readability measure. A function that fits on one screen (roughly 30 lines) is easy to understand at a glance. A function that spans multiple screens forces you to scroll back and forth to understand it. Long functions usually violate the Single Responsibility Principle — they do too many things.

Nesting depth is how many levels of if/for/while blocks are nested inside each other. Deep nesting forces readers to track multiple conditions simultaneously. A common refactoring technique is the early return: instead of if (valid) { ... }, return early on invalid: if (!valid) return;. This flattens the code.

Parameter count: functions with more than 5 parameters are hard to call correctly — it's easy to pass arguments in the wrong order. Group related parameters into a struct or class.

code_health.title: Code Duplication
code_health.html:
Code duplication (or copy-paste code) is when the same sequence of lines appears in multiple places. It accumulates when developers copy a working block rather than extracting it into a reusable function.

Why it's dangerous: when a bug is found in the duplicated code, it must be fixed in every copy. Often, some copies are forgotten — so the bug persists in the forgotten copies. The same applies to improvements: add a feature to one copy, and the others fall behind.

The fix: extract the duplicated block into a function and call it from all sites. Now there's one place to fix, one place to improve.

3% duplication is acceptable (small files, short similar setup blocks). 3–10% warrants attention. >10% means significant technical debt.

code_health.title: Dead Code
code_health.html:
Dead code is code that is present but never executed. It accumulates over a project's life as features are removed, refactored, or replaced.

Three forms:

Unreachable code — code after a return, break, or throw that can never execute.

Unused variables — variables assigned a value that is never read.

Unused functions — functions defined but never called.

Dead code is harmful because it confuses readers ("why is this here? does it do something I'm missing?"), increases binary size, and must be maintained for no benefit. When a reader finds dead code they don't understand, they often leave it in case it's needed — making the problem worse.

When you remove dead code, the codebase shrinks and becomes clearer. Version control preserves the history if you ever need it back.

code_health.title: Naming Conventions
code_health.html:
Good names make code self-documenting. Bad names force readers to look up definitions and track meaning externally. The conventions below are widely agreed upon.

Functions should be verbs or verb-noun pairs: calculateTotal, save_file, isValid. A function name should say what it does.

Classes and types should be nouns: UserAccount, FileParser, Rectangle.

Constants should be UPPER_CASE: MAX_RETRIES, DEFAULT_TIMEOUT.

Python: functions and variables use snake_case (my_function). C++/Java: functions use camelCase (myFunction). Mixing styles within a single file is confusing — pick one and be consistent.

Single-letter variable names (except loop counters i, j, k and coordinates x, y) obscure intent. d tells you nothing; duration tells you everything.

code_health.title: Overall Grade
code_health.html:
The overall grade (A–F) combines all five metrics:

A — all five metrics green. Your code is in excellent shape.

B — no red metrics, up to two yellow. Good code with minor rough edges.

C — up to one red or several yellows. Attention needed; maintainability is declining.

D — two or more red metrics. Significant issues; refactoring recommended before adding more features.

F — three or more red metrics. The codebase is fragile; new work is high-risk until health improves.

The grade is a snapshot, not a judgment on you as a developer. All codebases accumulate debt over time. The health check helps you see where to focus your next cleanup effort.

cards.heading: Code is Instructions
cards.body: Code is a list of instructions that tells a computer what to do, step by step. Like a recipe -- the computer follows it exactly.

cards.heading: Why Text?
cards.body: You could click buttons in a visual tool, but text is faster, more precise, and what every professional uses. Every app on your phone was written as text.

cards.heading: Languages
cards.body: Just like human languages, there are many programming languages. Each has strengths. Python is easy to read. C is fast. JavaScript runs in browsers. You pick the one that fits your job.

cards.heading: Variables
cards.body: A variable is a named container. price = 12.99 stores the number 12.99 under the name "price". You can read it, change it, and use it later.

cards.heading: Types
cards.body: Types describe what kind of data something is. 42 is an integer (whole number). 3.14 is a float (decimal). "hello" is a string (text). true is a boolean (yes/no).

cards.heading: Why Types Matter
cards.body: You can add two numbers: 5 + 3 = 8. You can add two strings: "hi" + " there" = "hi there". But 5 + "hi" doesn't make sense -- the type tells the computer what "add" means.

cards.heading: Functions
cards.body: A function is a reusable block of code with a name. calculate_total(prices) takes a list of prices and returns the total. You write it once, call it as many times as you want.

cards.heading: Parameters and Returns
cards.body: Parameters are the inputs (what you pass in). Return values are the outputs (what comes back). add(3, 7) passes 3 and 7 in, gets 10 back.

cards.heading: Methods
cards.body: A method is a function that belongs to an object. myList.append(5) -- append is a method on the list. Same idea as a function, just attached to something.

cards.heading: If/Else
cards.body: Decisions. if temperature > 100: alarm() -- the code only runs when the condition is true. else handles the other case.

cards.heading: Loops
cards.body: Repeating things. for item in list: process(item) -- runs the body once for every item. Without loops, you'd copy-paste the same code hundreds of times.

cards.heading: While Loops
cards.body: while not done: keep_trying() -- repeats until a condition changes. Useful when you don't know how many times you'll need to loop.

cards.heading: Structs / Types
cards.body: A struct groups related data together. An Item struct might have a name (string) and price (float). Instead of two separate variables, you have one thing with two fields.

cards.heading: Classes and Objects
cards.body: A class is a struct that also has functions (methods) attached. An object is one instance of a class. class Dog defines the template. myDog = Dog("Rex") creates one specific dog.

cards.heading: Inheritance
cards.body: A class can extend another. class Poodle extends Dog -- Poodle gets everything Dog has, plus its own additions. Not all languages have this -- C doesn't. Python and UL do.

cards.heading: Polymorphism
cards.body: Using a parent type to handle different children. A variable typed as Animal can hold a Dog, Cat, or Bird. The right method runs based on what's actually stored. This is how plugins and frameworks work.

cards.heading: What's an Algorithm?
cards.body: A step-by-step recipe for solving a problem. "Sort this list from smallest to largest" is a problem. Bubble sort, merge sort, quicksort are algorithms -- different recipes for the same result, with different speeds.

cards.heading: Big O Notation
cards.body: A way to describe how slow something gets as the input grows. O(n) means the time grows linearly -- twice the data, twice the time. O(n^2) means it gets much worse. You don't need to memorize this, but knowing it exists helps you understand why some code is slow.

cards.heading: You Already Use Them
cards.body: Every time you search, sort, filter, or deduplicate data -- that's an algorithm. Libraries like Python's sorted() use optimized algorithms so you don't have to write them yourself.

cards.heading: The Call Stack
cards.body: When a function calls another function, the computer remembers where it was. This stack of "return addresses" is the call stack. When the inner function finishes, execution returns to where it left off. Stack overflow = too many nested calls.

cards.heading: Compiled vs Interpreted
cards.body: Compiled (C, Rust): your code is translated to machine code BEFORE it runs. The output is a standalone binary. Interpreted (Python): your code is read and executed line by line by another program (the interpreter).

cards.heading: JIT vs AOT
cards.body: AOT (Ahead of Time): compile everything before running. C does this. JIT (Just in Time): compile hot paths while running. Java and JavaScript do this. JIT can be fast but uses more memory at startup.

cards.heading: VMs and Bytecode
cards.body: Some languages (Java, Python) compile to an intermediate format (bytecode), then a virtual machine interprets it. The VM is a program that pretends to be a computer. Slower than native code, but portable -- runs anywhere the VM exists.

cards.heading: What is Memory?
cards.body: RAM -- temporary, fast storage. Every variable, object, and string lives in memory while your program runs. When the program exits, it's all gone.

cards.heading: Stack vs Heap
cards.body: The stack is small, fast, automatic -- local variables go here. The heap is large, slower, manual -- objects you create with new or malloc go here. Python puts everything on the heap. C lets you choose.

cards.heading: Garbage Collection
cards.body: Some languages (Python, Java, Go) automatically find and free memory you're no longer using. You never think about it. The downside: the GC pauses your program briefly to do its work.

cards.heading: Manual Memory
cards.body: In C, YOU allocate (malloc) and free (free). Forget to free = memory leak (your program slowly eats all RAM). Free twice = crash. Use after free = security vulnerability.

cards.heading: Memory Safety
cards.body: The #1 source of security bugs is memory errors in C/C++. Rust solves this with ownership rules. UL lets you pick your model. Python avoids it entirely with GC.

cards.heading: What is a Platform?
cards.body: A platform is an OS + CPU architecture combination. Windows x64, macOS ARM64, Linux x64 are platforms. Code compiled for one platform doesn't run on another -- the machine instructions are different.

cards.heading: ISA (Instruction Set Architecture)
cards.body: The CPU's language. x64 (Intel/AMD) and ARM64 (Apple Silicon, phones) speak different instruction sets. A binary compiled for x64 is gibberish to an ARM chip. This is why you download different versions of software for different machines.

cards.heading: Why C/C++ Must Target Each Platform
cards.body: C compiles to native machine code for a specific ISA. To support Windows, Mac, and Linux, you compile three separate times. Python avoids this -- the interpreter handles platform differences. The trade-off: Python is slower.

cards.heading: LLVM and IR
cards.body: LLVM is a compiler toolkit. It takes an intermediate representation (IR) -- a platform-neutral format -- and compiles it to any ISA. Write one compiler front-end, get every platform for free. Rust, Swift, and UL use LLVM.

cards.heading: Assembly
cards.body: The human-readable form of machine code. MOV RAX, 5 means "put 5 in register RAX". You almost never write this directly, but debuggers show it when things go wrong at the lowest level.

cards.heading: Git
cards.body: A system that tracks every change you make to your code. You can go back to any previous version, see who changed what, and work on multiple features simultaneously without breaking each other's work.

cards.heading: Commit
cards.body: A snapshot of your code at a point in time with a message describing what changed. git commit -m "fix login bug". Your project history is a chain of commits.

cards.heading: Push and Pull
cards.body: Push: upload your commits to a remote server (GitHub). Pull: download other people's commits. This is how teams collaborate -- everyone pushes and pulls from the same repository.

cards.heading: GitHub
cards.body: A website that hosts Git repositories. It adds code review (pull requests), issue tracking, CI/CD (automatic testing), and collaboration features. Most open-source software lives on GitHub.

cards.heading: Branches
cards.body: A branch is a parallel timeline. You create a branch to work on a feature without touching the main code. When it's ready, you merge it back. If it doesn't work out, you delete the branch -- main is untouched.

cards.heading: Python
cards.body: Easy to read, huge ecosystem, slow for CPU work. Used for: AI/ML, data science, scripting, web backends, automation. The most popular first language.

cards.heading: JavaScript
cards.body: The language of the web browser. Every website uses it. Also runs on servers (Node.js). Dynamic, flexible, quirky. Used for: websites, web apps, mobile (React Native), servers.

cards.heading: C
cards.body: The foundation. Operating systems, databases, embedded devices. Fast as possible, zero overhead. Manual memory. Dangerous if you're not careful. 50+ years old and still everywhere.

cards.heading: C++
cards.body: C with classes, templates, and RAII. Used for: game engines (Unreal), browsers (Chrome), databases, performance-critical systems. Complex but powerful.

cards.heading: Rust
cards.body: Memory safety without garbage collection. The compiler enforces ownership rules -- if it compiles, it's safe. Used for: systems programming, CLI tools, WebAssembly. Steep learning curve.

cards.heading: Java
cards.body: Enterprise workhorse. Runs on the JVM -- write once, run anywhere. Verbose but reliable. Used for: Android apps, enterprise backends, big data (Hadoop/Spark).

cards.heading: Go
cards.body: Google's language for servers. Simple, fast compilation, great concurrency. Used for: cloud infrastructure (Docker, Kubernetes), microservices, CLIs.

cards.heading: UniLogic
cards.body: Write once, compile to C, Python, JS, WASM, or bytecode. Configurable memory and concurrency. Designed for people who want to understand what's happening under the hood.

cards.heading: APIs
cards.body: An API (Application Programming Interface) is how programs talk to each other. When your app fetches weather data, it calls a weather API -- sending a request and getting structured data back.

cards.heading: Debugging
cards.body: Finding and fixing bugs. Read the error message. Check the line number. Add print statements. Use a debugger to step through line by line. 90% of debugging is reading carefully.

cards.heading: Testing
cards.body: Writing code that checks your other code. assert add(2,3) == 5. If someone breaks the add function later, the test catches it immediately. Professional code has thousands of tests.

cards.heading: Dependencies
cards.body: Libraries other people wrote that your code uses. pip install requests gives you HTTP in Python. The risk: dependencies can break, get abandoned, or have security holes. Keep them updated.

cards.heading: The Terminal
cards.body: A text interface to your computer. You type commands, it executes them. Faster than clicking through menus once you learn it. Every developer uses it daily.

interactive_topics.title: Types & Variables
interactive_topics.subtitle: What data is, and how programs store and name it.
teaching: A variable is a named container. When you write price = 12.99, you create a container called price and put the number 12.99 inside it. You can read it, change it, and use it anywhere later in your code.

Types describe what kind of data a variable holds:
  42 → int (whole number)
  3.14 → float (decimal)
  "hello" → string (text)
  True / False → bool (yes/no)

code_blocks.code:
# Python
age    = 25        # int
score  = 9.8       # float
name   = "Alice"   # string
active = True      # bool
print(age, score, name, active)

exercises.question: What type is x = 3.14?
exercises.explanation: Correct! 3.14 has a decimal point so it's a float.

exercises.question: If x = 5 and y = 3, what does x + y evaluate to?
exercises.explanation: Correct! 5 + 3 = 8. Adding two ints always gives an int.

interactive_topics.title: Functions
interactive_topics.subtitle: Reusable blocks of code you can call by name.
teaching: A function is a named block of code you write once and call many times. It takes parameters (inputs) and may return a result (output). Functions let you avoid copy-pasting the same logic everywhere.

In Python, you declare functions with def. In C, you must specify the type of every parameter and the return type. Rust uses fn. In all cases, the idea is the same: give it a name, list inputs, and return something.

code_blocks.code:
# Python
def add(a, b):
    return a + b

result = add(3, 7)   # result = 10
print(result)

exercises.question:
Given this Python function:
def double(n):
    return n * 2

What does double(6) return?
exercises.explanation: Correct! 6 * 2 = 12. The function multiplies its input by 2.

exercises.question:
What is the return type of this C function?
float average(float a, float b) { return (a + b) / 2.0f; }
exercises.explanation: Correct! The return type float is declared before the function name in C.

interactive_topics.title: If / Else Logic
interactive_topics.subtitle: Making decisions in code.
teaching: An if statement runs a block of code only when a condition is true. An else block runs when the condition is false. You can chain conditions with elif (Python) or else if (C/Rust).
Conditions are expressions that evaluate to True or False. Common comparisons: == (equal), != (not equal), > (greater), < (less), >= (greater or equal).

exercises.question:
What does this print?
x = 10
if x > 5:
    print("big")
else:
    print("small")
exercises.explanation: Correct! 10 > 5 is True, so "big" is printed.

exercises.question: What operator checks if two values are equal?
exercises.explanation: Correct! == compares equality. A single = is for assignment, not comparison.

interactive_topics.title: Loops
interactive_topics.subtitle: Repeating actions efficiently.
teaching: A for loop iterates over a collection or a range of numbers, running its body once per item. A while loop repeats as long as a condition is true.
Without loops, you'd copy-paste code manually. With loops, you can process a million items with the same three lines of code.

code_blocks.code:
# Python — for loop
fruits = ["apple", "banana", "cherry"]
for fruit in fruits:
    print(fruit)

# while loop
count = 0
while count < 3:
    print(count)
    count += 1

exercises.question:
How many times does this loop run?
for i in range(4):
    print(i)
What keyword is used to exit a loop early in most languages?
exercises.explanation: Correct! break immediately exits the innermost loop.

interactive_topics.title: Collections
interactive_topics.subtitle: Storing multiple values together.
teaching: A list (Python) or array (C) stores multiple values in a sequence, accessed by index starting at 0. A dictionary (Python) or hash map stores key-value pairs — look up values by key instead of by position.
Choosing the right collection matters: lists are for ordered sequences, sets for fast membership checking, dictionaries for key-value mapping.

code_blocks.code:
# Python — list
scores = [95, 82, 71, 90]
print(scores[0])   # 95 (first element)
scores.append(88)  # add to end

# dictionary
person = {"name": "Alice", "age": 25}
print(person["name"])   # Alice

exercises.question: Given items = [10, 20, 30], what is items[2]?
exercises.explanation: Correct! Indices start at 0, so index 2 is the third element: 30.

exercises.question: What method adds an item to the end of a Python list?
exercises.explanation: Correct! list.append(value) adds the value to the end.

interactive_topics.title: Objects & Inheritance
interactive_topics.subtitle: Bundling data and behaviour together.
teaching: A class is a blueprint for creating objects. It bundles related data (fields) and behaviour (methods) together. An object is one specific instance of a class.
Inheritance lets one class extend another, inheriting all its fields and methods. The child class can add new ones or override existing ones. This avoids duplicating shared logic.

exercises.question: In Python, what keyword is used to inherit from a parent class?
options: Shown in parentheses after class name
exercises.explanation: Correct! Python inherits by putting the parent in parentheses: class Dog(Animal):

exercises.question: What is it called when a child class provides its own version of a parent's method?
exercises.explanation: Correct! Method overriding lets a child class replace the parent's implementation.

interactive_topics.title: Language Deep Dive
interactive_topics.subtitle: How your selected languages compare at a deeper level.
teaching: Every language makes trade-offs. Python is simple but slow. C is fast but manual. Rust is safe and fast but strict. UniLogic is configurable — you choose the trade-offs at the top of each file.
The best language for a task depends on: performance requirements, team familiarity, ecosystem (available libraries), deployment target, and how much control vs. safety you want.

exercises.question: Which language uses garbage collection to manage memory automatically?
exercises.explanation: Correct! Python uses reference counting plus a cyclic garbage collector. You never call malloc or free.

exercises.question: What makes Rust's memory safety unique compared to Python and C?
options: It uses a GC like Python
It uses ownership rules enforced at compile time
It has no memory management at all
exercises.explanation: Correct! Rust's ownership/borrow checker enforces memory safety at compile time — no GC needed, no manual free() needed.
